summary: This Environment & Urbanization book note reviews Responsible Living: Concepts, Education and Future Perspectives, a 2015 Springer volume edited by Victoria W Thoresen, Robert J Didham, Jørgen Klein and Declan Doyle. The book examines how education, in many countries and formats, can help individuals move toward sustainable development and close the value-action gap. The note also raises philosophical questions about context, the good life, and whether personal fulfilment is a privilege, while noting the book explores both the power and limits of transformational education.
one_line: Book note on a 2015 Springer volume examining education for sustainability and how individuals can close the gap between values and responsible action.
key_facts: Responsible Living: Concepts, Education and Future Perspectives was published by Springer in 2015 and runs to 283 pages.
The book's editors are Victoria W Thoresen, Robert J Didham, Jørgen Klein and Declan Doyle.
The book is concerned with how individuals can guide the transition toward sustainable development, with education seen as essential to this.
The book's chapters cover education for sustainability in a wide range of countries and use tools such as formal curricula, social media, workshops, exhibitions, activism and games.
The Supporting Urban Sustainability (SUS) programme has been implemented in 14 countries in Africa, Asia and Europe.
SUS gathers civil society and local government officials to learn about and act on urban poverty alleviation based on ecosystem services.
The note argues that without broader educational agendas, the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) risk being a lofty exercise that many ordinary people feel is irrelevant to them.
The 'value-action gap' is the situation where many people profess to want to lead more responsible lifestyles, yet what they say does not match what they do.
Research has found individuals may be more motivated to turn values into actions if presented with the positive consequences of doing so, rather than dwelling on bleak scenarios.
In Sierra Leone, discussing the existence of the value-action gap among youth discussing post-conflict discrimination was shown to help mitigate it.
The note states that capturing emotional, not just intellectual, drivers of behavioural change is key to closing the value-action gap.
The note questions whether having a sense of purpose and being empowered to contribute socially are only the preserve of the privileged.
The book note was prepared by Christine Ro and is part of the Book notes section of Environment and Urbanization, published by Sage and prepared by the IIED Human Settlements research group.
